definition: The on-accelerator high-bandwidth memory holding weights, activations, and KV cache.
details: The on-accelerator high-bandwidth memory holding weights, activations, and KV cache. The binding constraint of LLM work: a 70B model in 16-bit needs ~140 GB for weights alone, before a single token of cache. Memory math (weights + cache + activations vs. available HBM) is the first calculation of every deployment.

explainer.lead: VRAM is the on-accelerator high-bandwidth memory that holds an LLM's weights, activations, and KV cache. It is the binding constraint of LLM work: a 70B model in 16-bit needs roughly 140 GB for weights alone, before any cache.

tiers.eli5: It is the fast, small workbench next to the processor; if your model and its notes do not fit on the bench, you cannot get the job done.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers start every deployment by computing weights plus cache plus activations against available HBM. A common pitfall is budgeting weights only and then running out of memory once the KV cache grows with context length.
tiers.paperLevel: Defined operationally as weights + cache + activations must fit within available HBM; a 16-bit 70B model requires about 140 GB for weights alone.

explainer.example: For a 70B model in 16-bit, the weights consume roughly 140 GB of VRAM, so the KV cache and activations must fit in whatever HBM remains.
